strings.coding.lede: Code real tax rules in one format: download a template, fill in the legal fields from the sources in a spreadsheet, and import the ZIP. Every legal row needs a source, a rule status and a verified flag; unverified rows can be used but are flagged on every result. The data dictionary in each template explains every column and its coding layer (liability, collection, observation).

strings.compare.corr: Do the measures rank jurisdictions alike?
strings.compare.k.agreed: Rankings on which all readings agree
strings.compare.lede: Puts the measures of each method side by side for every jurisdiction, without merging them into one score. Where a paper can be read in more than one way, each reading is run; a jurisdiction gets a rank only if every reading gives the same one, and otherwise the range is shown. Classifications show how many readings support them.
strings.compare.lede.tech: Namespaced measures by jurisdiction under every documented reading (vtrl2018 I2 × I8; gb2017 I1 × I5; ph defaults). Agreement rule (plan s 6.3): a rank only where all readings agree, otherwise a tie with the range; robustness shares of gb2017 classifications; Spearman and Kendall tau-b on default readings. No combined score. Specification docs/specs/compare_models.md v0.1.
strings.compare.no_classes: No jurisdiction is classified as a sink or conduit under any reading.
strings.compare.readings_note: Readings are the documented alternative interpretations of each paper. Other settings stay at their defaults; change them on each method's own page.
strings.compare.robust: How many readings support each classification
strings.compare.title: Compare the methods
strings.conduits.lede: Finds jurisdictions where a disproportionate share of corporate value ends up (sinks) and those through which value passes on its way to or from them (conduits), following Garcia-Bernardo and others (2017). Move the thresholds and the classification recomputes at once.
strings.conduits.lede.tech: Reproduction of Garcia-Bernardo, Fichtner, Takes and Heemskerk (2017): firm-level ownership chains weighted by the owned firm's revenue times multiplicative ownership, aggregated to country chains; sink centrality on G2 and inward and outward conduit centralities on G3, each relative to GDP share. Specification v0.1 (draft).

strings.conduits.title: Conduits and sinks
strings.conduits.title.plain: Where value ends up, and where it passes through

strings.guide.compare.corr.plain: How similarly two measures rank the jurisdictions: 1 means the same order, 0 no relation, −1 the reverse order. Measures from different methods need not agree; they measure different things.
strings.guide.compare.corr.tech: Spearman's ρ on each measure's default reading over jurisdictions where both are defined; Kendall's τ-b is in the CSV export.
strings.guide.compare.grid.plain: Each row is a jurisdiction and each column a measure from one of the methods. A number is the jurisdiction's rank on that measure (1 is highest) when every reading of the paper agrees; a range such as 2–4 means the readings disagree, so no rank is claimed. Dashes mean the measure is undefined there.
strings.guide.compare.grid.tech: Agreement rule: competition rank under each reading; coloured cells are agreed ranks, uncoloured cells show the range across readings; '–' is unranked in every reading.
strings.guide.compare.robust.plain: For each jurisdiction classed as a sink or a conduit under at least one reading: the share of the four readings of Garcia-Bernardo and others under which it is. A full bar means the classification does not depend on how the paper is read.
strings.guide.compare.robust.tech: Robustness share = readings classifying the jurisdiction / readings run (I1 × I5).
strings.guide.compare.sensitivity.plain: The chosen measure for every jurisdiction under each reading of the paper. Points that sit on top of one another mean the reading makes no difference.
strings.guide.compare.sensitivity.tech: Values by reading for the selected measure; divergence identifies interpretation-sensitive jurisdictions.
strings.guide.conduits.sankey.plain: Value travelling through chains of three countries: where it starts (left), which country it passes through (middle) and where it ends (right). Thick bands show the largest flows.
strings.guide.conduits.sankey.tech: The 60 largest G3 country chains by value, drawn as origin, middle and last country; link colour by the middle country.
strings.guide.conduits.scatter.plain: Each bubble is a country. Further right: more value passes through it on the way to sink countries. Higher up: more value from sink countries passes through it. Countries in the shaded corner do both, and are classed as conduits. Red bubbles are sinks.
strings.guide.conduits.scatter.tech: Outward against inward conduit centrality (log axes; values at or below 0.01, including undefined, are pinned to the floor). Colour: sink centrality; size: GDP; shaded area: both above the conduit threshold.
strings.guide.conduits.sink.plain: How much more corporate value ends up in each country than the size of its economy would suggest. Bars above the dotted line are classed as sinks.
strings.guide.conduits.sink.tech: S_c = net G2 value share divided by GDP share (reconstruction I4); dotted line: sink threshold.
strings.guide.matrix.heatmap.plain: Each cell shows how strongly companies in one country (row) hold companies in another (column). Brighter cells mean more, or larger, holdings.
strings.guide.matrix.heatmap.tech: Holder-jurisdiction by held-jurisdiction matrix of the chosen aggregation (count, sum of fractions or sum of values, single currency enforced). The diagonal holds domestic relations when included.
strings.guide.network.graph.plain: Dots are companies, coloured by country; arrows are ownership links, coloured and thickened by size. Switch to the value-flow view to follow profits towards the owners, or to the country view to see links between jurisdictions.
strings.guide.network.graph.tech: Ownership view: holder to held; value-flow view: held to holder; jurisdiction view: aggregated under the stated rule. Layout: jurisdictions on a circle, entities on rings. Parallel relations are separate edges.
strings.guide.overview.entities.plain: Each bar is a jurisdiction; the coloured blocks show how many of its companies are parents, holding, finance or operating companies. A tall bar of holding companies in a small jurisdiction is the kind of pattern worth exploring further.
strings.guide.overview.entities.tech: Count of entities by jurisdiction_id and entity_type, current dataset version. Entity types follow each record's entity_type_rule.
strings.guide.overview.fractions.plain: How much of a company each ownership link represents. Most links in group structures are full or majority holdings; small stakes are usually portfolio holdings.
strings.guide.overview.fractions.tech: Histogram of the fraction column of current direct relations (valid_to empty), in bands; relations without a reported fraction are omitted, never imputed.
strings.guide.routes.centrality.plain: How often each country lies on the cheapest routes between other countries, weighted by the size of their economies. High bars are the main conduit countries in this world.
strings.guide.routes.centrality.tech: BTWNS over routes within the tolerance, STRCT over strictly cheapest routes, OCCUR as weighted presence; pair weights GDP_S x GDP_P normalised to 100 (I8).
strings.guide.routes.decomposition.plain: The blue part is the host country's company tax, paid whichever way the money goes. The upper part is the extra tax on sending profits home: compare the direct route with the cheapest one.
strings.guide.routes.decomposition.tech: t^e = t_S + (1 - t_S) d, split into host CIT and the route's tax distance contribution, for the direct and the cheapest route.
strings.guide.routes.map.plain: Profits earned in the host country (red ring) travel to the home country (green ring). The coloured line is the cheapest way through other countries; the dashed line is the direct route. Darker legs add little tax, brighter legs add more.
strings.guide.routes.map.tech: Cheapest route by Dijkstra on -ln(1-d) plus a penalty per intermediate; leg colour by d. Conduit legs use the world-average CIT excluding the conduit where the next parent gives credit (spec s 5).
strings.guide.routes.shop.plain: For every pair of countries, how much tax a detour through other countries saves compared with the direct route. Bright cells are where treaty shopping pays most. Click a cell to open that pair.
strings.guide.routes.shop.tech: SHOP = t^e(direct) - t^e(cheapest), host by row, home by column (interpretation I10).
strings.guide.topology.barcode.plain: The same shapes as bars, from the scale at which each appears to the scale at which it disappears. Long bars are robust. Bars crossing the dotted line exist at the chosen scale. Click a bar to select it.
strings.guide.topology.barcode.tech: Barcode of all H1 bars and the 30 longest H0 bars; opacity marks bars alive at ε.
strings.guide.topology.betti.plain: How many separate groups (blue, left axis) and loops (orange, right axis) there are at each scale. At small scales every jurisdiction is its own group; as the scale grows they merge into one.
strings.guide.topology.betti.tech: β0(ε) and β1(ε) as step functions of the scale.
strings.guide.topology.diagram.plain: Each mark is a shape: blue for a group, orange for a loop. Across: the scale at which it appears; up: the scale at which it disappears. Marks far above the diagonal last a long time and are the robust features; marks close to it are noise. The shaded corner holds the shapes present at the chosen scale. Click a loop to trace it on the map.
strings.guide.topology.diagram.tech: Persistence diagram: (birth, death) for H0 and H1; triangles at the top are essential classes. Shaded region: classes alive at ε (birth ≤ ε < death). Bottleneck stability: perturbing distances by δ moves the diagram by at most δ.
strings.guide.topology.influence.plain: How much the shapes change when one jurisdiction is left out. A tall orange bar means the loops depend on that jurisdiction.
strings.guide.topology.influence.tech: Bottleneck distance between the diagram of all observations and the diagram without the jurisdiction, for H0 and H1 (spec s 5.3).
strings.guide.topology.map.plain: Each dot is a jurisdiction. Two jurisdictions are joined by a line when they are within the chosen scale of each other; dots of the same colour form one group at that scale. A thick orange line traces the selected loop. The picture is a flattened view of many characteristics, so distances on screen are approximate; the stress value says how approximate (0 is exact).
strings.guide.topology.map.tech: Classical MDS projection (display only, D4; Kruskal stress-1 shown). Edges: pairs with d ≤ ε in the input metric; colours: connected components of VR(ε); thick line: a representative cycle of the selected H1 class.

strings.topology.ip_note: This page uses persistent homology, one of the alternatives recorded in plan s 9.4. The patented topological pipeline (US 10,417,262) stays blocked behind its IP gate; see Methods.
strings.topology.k.influential: Jurisdiction the loops depend on most
strings.topology.lede: Treats each jurisdiction as a point, placed by its tax and network characteristics, and asks what shape the points make as you look at them from close up to far away: which groups form and when they merge, and whether jurisdictions surround a gap, forming a loop. Long-lived shapes are the robust ones. Move the scale to see the structure at one distance; change the inputs and everything recomputes.
strings.topology.lede.tech: Persistent homology of the Vietoris–Rips filtration of a declared feature matrix (or of symmetrised tax-routing cost): H0 by union-find, H1 by persistent cohomology with clearing; bottleneck distance for leave-one-out influence. Specification docs/specs/ph_vietoris_rips.md v0.1. No lens, cover or cluster graph (design constraints D1 to D5).
strings.topology.map.tech: Rips graph at scale ε on a display projection
